key_insight: The paper argues that the main bottleneck in autonomous scientific discovery is no longer the agent workflow, but the environment it operates in. By engineering the right resources, constraints, and interfaces, LLM agents can more effectively generate, test, and improve scientific ideas.
problem_solved: Current LLM agent systems for science often focus on fixed workflows, which can limit discovery performance. This paper addresses how to better support autonomous scientific discovery by designing the surrounding execution environment instead of manually prescribing every agent step.
method: Frame scientific discovery as an agent-environment optimization problem, where the environment provides the resources and constraints for exploration.
Use optimized execution settings to let agents propose hypotheses, validate them, and iterate toward better solutions.
Shift emphasis from hand-crafted multi-step workflows to environment design that enables scalable, autonomous experimentation.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this reframes how to build scientific agents: better environments may matter more than more complex prompting or orchestration. It suggests a practical path to stronger autonomous discovery systems with less manual workflow engineering.
visual_elements: A pipeline diagram showing agent -> environment -> hypothesis -> validation -> iteration
A comparison graphic: workflow engineering vs environment engineering
An icon-based illustration of resources, constraints, and interfaces inside the agent environment
A loop chart showing repeated scientific discovery cycles and performance improvement
paper_title: EurekAgent: Agent Environment Engineering is All You Need For Autonomous Scientific Discovery
paper_authors: Amy Xin, Jiening Siow, Junjie Wang, Zijun Yao, Fanjin Zhang
